brief: The AI trade shows stress: CoreWeave imploded in October, Jensen Huang exited Nvidia, banks are pulling back from chip-backed loans, and Anthropic's IPO coincided with the S&P falling below its 200-day average. Yet GPU rental prices keep rising (Silicon Data's B200 index up 23.5% since late August, H100 up 67% since mid-2025), which Michael Dell and Nvidia read as proof demand is strong. Liquid Compute's Stanley Lee argues the rise is instead a credit story. Advance rates on neocloud GPU loans fell from 80% loan-to-value over the summer to about 70% after Labor Day to 50-60% now. Neoclouds that cannot get term financing cannot sell buyers long-term contracts, so those buyers are forced into a thin, visible spot market and bid it up, while operators who cannot finance new clusters build less. Neither effect requires new revenue. Supporting evidence: wide same-day price dispersion across providers, lenders newly worried about concentrated exposure to a few AI offtakers, rising demand for index put options, and token prices falling even as rental costs climb. Goldman's own most important metric in the AI trade rose at the same time AI credit spreads blew out. The author sides with credit over the chart.
